The Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 was introduced to address the erosion of law enforcement and security agencies' investigative capacity due to encryption, creating new industry assistance powers (technical assistance and technical capability notices) without mandating backdoors, expanding computer access warrants, and increasing penalties for failing to assist device access—citing that encryption affected 9 in 10 ASIO priority cases and 200 AFP operations, and encrypted intercepts rose from 3% in June 2013 to over 55% by July 2017.

Labor supported the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 after negotiating amendments to define “systemic weakness,” strengthen oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Commonwealth Ombudsman, and require further review, in order to address risks to national security, US security cooperation, and Australian technology businesses.

The speaker argued that the bill creates a systemic weakness in encrypted communications, threatening privacy, the tech industry, and civil liberties. They opposed rushed passage of the bill and the 50 pages of last-minute amendments, citing past failures like metadata laws that saw 350,000 requests per year, and warned that Australia would become a place where tech developers would avoid working.

Argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 addressed serious terrorism, child abuse, security and privacy issues, but criticised the government's handling and contradictory explanations. Supported targeted assistance powers while opposing systemic weaknesses, back doors and weakened encryption, and backed stronger Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security safeguards.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 risks weakening encryption without adequate judicial oversight, warning that 350,000 metadata requests—including from local councils—demonstrate how security powers can be misused.

The speaker argued the government rushed and politicised the encryption bill, refused judicial oversight for technical assistance and capability notices, and failed to define 'systemic weakness'. Labor reached a compromise to pass the bill before Christmas but maintained concerns.

Opposed the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing it would build a known vulnerability into encryption software that could be exploited by wrongdoers, and criticised the excessive extension of state power through security reforms including mandatory metadata retention. Also defended the member for Eden-Monaro’s comments and described the member for Hume’s comment as deeply offensive.

The MP criticised the government for rushing the encryption bill without proper consultation, arguing Labor secured amendments to clarify systemic weakness, add oversight by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security and the Ombudsman, and require Attorney-General and communications minister approval for technical capability notices. Labor remains concerned about the lack of judicial oversight for interception-related notices and will monitor the legislation, with the committee inquiry continuing into 2019 and a separate review by the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor within 18 months.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 requires balancing national security with individual privacy, noting that the government rushed the bill through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security despite bipartisan efforts and 300 amendments on 15 previous national security bills. The speaker criticized Prime Minister Morrison and the Minister for Home Affairs for politicizing the process and ignoring submissions from Australian tech companies, while Labor proposed substantive amendments to address concerns from industry and civil society.

The speaker argued that the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018 is urgently needed to help law enforcement and national security agencies access encrypted communications used by criminals and terrorists, citing that 95% of ASIO’s top counterterrorism targets use encryption and referencing recent fatal attacks in Melbourne. The bill introduces new computer access warrants and industry assistance frameworks, prohibits systemic backdoors, and includes safeguards against mass surveillance, with the speaker urging parliamentary support for the bill and agreed amendments.

The speaker criticised the government's handling of the Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Bill 2018, arguing that the process was rushed and interfered with despite a consensus report from the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security. They noted the bill is 175 pages, amends 10 acts, and introduces new compulsory powers against innocent third parties, and that the government tabled 173 amendments (covering 50 pages) informally at 6:30 am on the day of debate, with no formal response to the committee's 17 recommendations.

The bill implements Australia's obligations under the TPP-11, which eliminates over 98% of tariffs in a $13.7 trillion trade zone covering nearly 500 million consumers, and the speaker urged Parliament to pass it quickly, criticising the Opposition Leader for previously declaring the deal dead after the US withdrawal.

Labor will support the CPTPP implementation bills but opposes the government's waiver of labour market testing for six countries and the inclusion of investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) clauses; if elected, Labor will seek to remove ISDS, reinstate labour market testing, require independent economic assessments of all trade deals, and strengthen parliamentary scrutiny.

The speaker supported the amendments to the CPTPP implementation bills proposed by the member for Blaxland, arguing for free trade that includes strong labour standards, environmental protections, and transparency, while opposing investor-state dispute settlement provisions and committing to restore labour market testing if Labor is elected.

The TPP-11 will eliminate over 98% of tariffs on Australian exports to 11 Asia-Pacific countries with a combined GDP of $13.8 trillion and 500 million consumers, delivering specific benefits such as the elimination of Canadian beef tariffs (currently 26.5%) within five years and Mexican beef tariffs (up to 25%) within ten years. The speaker argued the agreement strengthens Australia’s free trade network, provides new opportunities for agricultural and service exporters, and does not weaken Australian labour, skills or regulatory standards.

The speaker argued in support of the Customs Amendment Bill to implement the TPP-11, criticising the Greens for hypocrisy on trade and stating the agreement would remove 98% of tariffs among 11 countries representing 500 million people and $13.8 trillion in combined GDP. He also highlighted the government's broader economic agenda, including personal income tax cuts, infrastructure investment, and small business support.

The speaker argued that the TPP-11 will eliminate tariffs with 11 countries worth $13.8 trillion combined GDP, boost exports for farmers, manufacturers, and service providers, and increase Australia's net national income by $15.5 billion by 2030.

The speaker supported the bill but argued for mandatory independent economic modelling, citing industry-commissioned research showing negligible GDP gains and zero agricultural benefits under TPP-11; they also called for an accredited trade advisers program, stronger parliamentary treaty scrutiny, and raised concerns about labour market testing waivers for six countries and skills testing risks in the electrical sector.

The speaker argued that the TPP-11 agreement delivers a good outcome for the sugar industry and creates jobs, naming six individuals in his electorate—Enio Troiani, David Pickering, Giuseppe Barazza, Rob Zahn, Leone Aslett and Scott Collins—who advanced from apprenticeships to management roles in Bundaberg's sugar sector.

Labor supported the CPTPP bill but criticised its investor-state dispute settlement provisions, labour market testing waivers, and lack of independent economic modelling; a future Shorten Labor government would remove ISDS, reinstate labour market testing, require independent modelling, enforce mandatory skills testing, and create an accredited trade advisers program.

The speaker opposed the Customs Amendment (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership Implementation) Bill 2018, arguing that investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) clauses allow foreign corporations to sue the Australian government and undermine parliamentary sovereignty, and that labour mobility provisions diminish control over immigration policy. They supported Labor's commitment to remove ISDS and fix these issues when in government.

The speaker opposed the Trans-Pacific Partnership bill, arguing it is a flawed preferential trade agreement that undermines Australian sovereignty through investor-state dispute settlement and lacks independent country-specific economic analysis, and stated Centre Alliance would not support it unless significant flaws are addressed.

The TPP-11 provides minimal economic benefit—0.5% GDP over 10 years—and gives away labour market testing for six countries while including problematic investor-state dispute settlement mechanisms and lacking independent economic analysis. Future US re-entry could also impose costly monopoly protections for biologic medicines.

The speaker called for the government to provide an independent economic analysis and transparency regarding the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, arguing that trade deals create winners and losers and that the current legislation lacks clear assumptions and review processes.

The speaker argued that the Customs Amendment (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership Implementation) Bill 2018 fails to include adequate labour market testing, supporting an amendment by the member for Blaxland, and cited the case of John Holland in Hobart failing to pay Chinese migrant workers for nine weeks.

Labor supported the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, along with the shadow trade minister's amendment, citing the agreement's side agreements on human rights, labour rights and the environment. The party raised concerns about investor-state dispute provisions—noting only Canada would newly be subject to them—and argued for transitional arrangements and investment in education and TAFE to keep Australian workers competitive.

The speaker argued for the swift passage of the TPP-11 implementing bills, stating the agreement would eliminate 98% of tariffs, deliver a $15.6 billion net annual benefit to national income by 2030, and give Australian beef exporters a 13 percentage point tariff advantage over US competitors in Japan within two years.

Returned from the House of Representatives

The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act to allow return of unlawful noncitizens without a visa in more circumstances, such as transit refusal or UN Human Rights Committee interim measures, and clarifies that visa application bars continue as if they never left. It also enables document delivery via online accounts, inserts a power to refund duty when overpaid, recovers merchant fees for credit card payments, and makes minor technical amendments to the Customs Act.

The speech supported the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 while accusing the Minister for Home Affairs of mismanagement. It cited partner visa processing times rising from 19 to 30 months for 90% of applications, more than 176,000 bridging visas, and an ANAO report finding only two of 33 consultant contracts were evaluated.

The Greens argued the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 contains provisions that bar asylum seekers returned to Australia after a third country refuses them from reapplying for protection, which the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights flagged as a human rights concern. The Greens will further examine the bill in the Senate and do not support it.

The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act 1958, Customs Act 1901, and Passenger Movement Charge Collection Act 1978. Key changes include allowing unlawful noncitizens returned to Australia after a failed removal to re-enter without a visa, permitting the Department of Home Affairs to use ImmiAccount for legal communications, enabling recoverable customs payments, controlling movement between sea installations and the coast, regulating disposal of narcotic-related goods, and prescribing fees for passenger movement charge collection.

The government moved to reject Senate amendments to the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing they would unconstitutionally increase public expenditure from standing appropriations by requiring the minister to appoint at least six doctors to a health panel. The speaker claimed Labor had supported the amendments in December 2018 without security agency advice, then withdrew support months later, and warned that accepting the amendments would breach 109 years of House of Representatives practice and section 53 of the Constitution by allowing the Senate to initiate spending.

The speaker moved an amendment to set aside constitutional disputes with the Senate over the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018, citing public interest in speedy passage, and noted that the Howard government had moved an identical resolution in November 1996.

The bill would give the Federal Circuit Court of Australia the power to issue injunctions or order compensation when a supplier breaks the Commonwealth Procurement Rules for a covered procurement.

A supplier would have to lodge a complaint with the relevant Commonwealth entity's accountable authority and have it investigated, and the procurement would be paused unless a public interest certificate is in force, before going to court.

The bill aims to help Australia meet its international trade obligations, such as those under the World Trade Organization Agreement on Government Procurement and the Trans-Pacific Partnership Agreement, and to give regional and small businesses easier access to justice.
Vests the Federal Circuit Court with jurisdiction to grant injunctions and order compensation for procurement rule breaches.
Requires suppliers to complain to the accountable authority first and have the procurement suspended during investigation, unless a public interest certificate applies.
Enables Australia to meet international obligations on government procurement complaints and remedies.
Suppliers, including regional and small and medium enterprises, and Commonwealth entities involved in covered procurements.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2018-10-18.83.1) to pass the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5871). In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1819a/19bd026): > *The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 (the Bill) proposes to fill a gap in the current arrangements in administrative law relating to Commonwealth procurement, and to address obligations under relevant free trade agreements, by creating new rules for making and investigating complaints in relation to the contravention of relevant Commonwealth Procurement Rules (CPRs).*

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill establishes an independent complaints mechanism for Commonwealth procurement, designating the Federal Circuit Court to review breaches of the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, with compensation limited to reasonable tender preparation costs, and requiring suppliers to first complain to the procuring entity.

Labor supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 to give small and medium businesses cheaper, faster court access for procurement disputes, but moved an amendment criticising the government for not maximising opportunities in the $50 billion annual procurement program.

The speaker supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 and an amendment, but criticised procurement policies for overlooking local economic benefits, citing the defence dress uniforms contract from Bendigo's Australian Defence Apparel being sent to Vietnam, costing 50–70 local jobs, and argued for greater local content and WTO standards to counter illegal dumping.

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 expands the Federal Circuit Court's jurisdiction to hear disputes under the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, allowing it to grant injunctions and order compensation for breaches. The speaker also argued that Commonwealth procurement should prioritise local Australian suppliers, particularly small and medium enterprises, and consider broader economic benefits like tax receipts and multiplier effects, not just immediate value for money.

The speaker supported the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 with an amendment but criticised its timing, arguing it should wait until WTO Government Procurement Agreement accession is resolved, and noted that past trade agreements like the Australia-US Free Trade Agreement underdelivered on Australian access to foreign contracts. The speech also highlighted $47–60 billion in annual Commonwealth procurement, risks to small and medium enterprises, and called for using procurement to achieve broader goals such as human rights compliance, environmental sustainability, and stronger Australian industry participation, citing weak requirements in the Future Submarine program.

The Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 adds an appeals mechanism to the Commonwealth Procurement Rules to comply with free trade agreements, but the speaker emphasised that Australian small and medium businesses face major barriers to winning government contracts, with Defence accounting for $112 billion of the $217 billion in procurement from 2012–13 to 2016–17, and the 10% SME target undermined by competition from international firms and costly panel arrangements.

The speaker argued that the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017, implementing Trans-Pacific Partnership and WTO Government Procurement Agreement commitments, weakens Australia's ability to favour local businesses by making it easier for foreign entities to challenge government contracts. The speaker noted that in 2015–16, Commonwealth agencies entered 70,338 contracts worth $56.9 billion, with total government procurement estimated at $120 billion annually, and criticised the government for not broadening 'value for money' to include whole-of-life benefits.

The member moved an amendment to defer the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 until the Trans-Pacific Partnership and WTO Agreement on Government Procurement include better protections for labour, the environment and local business and remove investor-state dispute settlement provisions. The bill was opposed on the grounds that it would let multinational corporations sue the Australian government, disadvantage local businesses, and was being rushed through without the final trade agreement text being seen.

The speaker argued that free trade policies have destroyed Australian manufacturing and agriculture, citing closures of the motor vehicle, whitegoods, textile, steel, cement, sugar, dairy and wool industries, with specific declines of 23% in beef, 31% in dairy and 72% in sheep numbers. He called for restoring sovereignty by requiring all government-procured motor vehicles to be Australian-made.

The speaker argued that the Government Procurement (Judicial Review) Bill 2017 creates an independent complaints mechanism for procurement, giving regional and small suppliers timely access to justice, and noted that 95% of contracts (worth $40.8 billion) were awarded to Australian suppliers in 2016–17.
Health Insurance Amendment (Medicare Funding for Certain Types of Abortion) Bill 2013

The order of general business was set to consider first the Health Insurance Amendment (Medicare Funding for Certain Types of Abortion) Bill 2013, then the Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013. The motion was agreed to.
Criminal Code Amendment (Misrepresentation of Age to a Minor) Bill 2013

The bills amend tax laws to tax excess concessional superannuation contributions at an individual's marginal rate instead of the top 46.5% rate, allow withdrawal of excess contributions, and apply from 1 July 2013; the change is estimated to reduce tax liability for about 40,000 low and middle income earners by around $1,100 on average in 2013-14.

The government introduced the Public Interest Disclosure Bill 2013 to create the first stand‑alone federal whistleblower protection scheme, enabling Commonwealth public officials to report suspected wrongdoing and receive protections against reprisal. The bill also established oversight roles for the Commonwealth Ombudsman and the Inspector‑General of Intelligence and Security, and a companion bill repealed existing whistleblower provisions in the Public Service Act 1999 and Parliamentary Service Act 1999.

The speaker moved three appropriation bills for 2013–2014, seeking a total of just under $184.8 million for parliamentary departments, just under $78.2 billion for ordinary annual services, and just under $4.8 billion for other government expenses, with details in the schedules.
National Disability Insurance Scheme Legislation Amendment Bill 2013

Moved to suspend standing orders so that 14 bills related to DisabilityCare Australia (the National Disability Insurance Scheme) could be considered during the current sitting period; the motion was agreed to.

The government argued for increasing the Medicare levy from 1.5% to 2% from July 2014 to fund DisabilityCare Australia, and announced the establishment of the DisabilityCare Australia Fund and technical amendments to the NDIS Act. The scheme will roll out from July 2013 in launch sites
